title: Finite-cover tube decomposition and identification of the ordinary comparison
statement:
Let $f:X\to S$ be finite type [def-weil-finite-type-morphism], $g:U\to S$ arbitrary, and $X_U=X\times_SU$. Let $\Lambda$ be a finite commutative ring killed by an integer invertible on $S$ and $K\in D^b_c(X_{\mathrm{Et}},\Lambda)$, in the constant-module category of [def-trf-oriented-nearby-cycles]. Choose $z_U=(x_U,b_U,c_U)$ in $V_{f_U}$ with image $z=(x,b,c)$ in $V_f$. Strict localizations and the chosen specializations define the tubes
$$M=X_{(x)}\times_{S_{(f(x))}}S_{(b)},\qquad N=(X_U)_{(x_U)}\times_{U_{(f_U(x_U))}}U_{(b_U)}.$$
There is a natural map $N\to M$. Under the oriented-point cohomology isomorphisms [lem-trf-oriented-point-cohomology], the stalk at $z_U$ of the ordinary comparison $\beta_g:v_g^*R\Psi_fK\to R\Psi_{f_U}K_U$ is the restriction map $R\Gamma(M,K)\to R\Gamma(N,K_U)$.

Put $S_0=S_{(f(x))}$, $U_0=U_{(f_U(x_U))}$ and let $P\to S_0$ be finite surjective. Set $P_q=P^{\times_{S_0}(q+1)}$, $Q_q=U_0\times_{S_0}P_q$, $A_q=R\Gamma(M\times_{S_0}P_q,K)$ and $B_q=R\Gamma(N\times_{U_0}Q_q,K_U)$. Both families have the restriction maps of their augmented Cech diagrams. Here $b$ and $b_U$ mean their lifts to $S_0$ and $U_0$ defined by $c$ and $c_U$. Write $a$ and $a_U$ for the closed geometric points of $S_0$ and $U_0$ defined by $f(x)$ and $f_U(x_U)$. For each $i\in I_q=\pi_0((P_q)_b)$ let $p_i$ be the projection of the unique geometric point of its component with the field of $b$. The decomposition of $P_q$ into finite strictly henselian local factors over $S_0$ [lem-trf-finite-base-strict-localization] puts the image of $p_i$ in a unique factor $H_{q,i}$ (different $i$ may give the same factor). Let $a_{q,i}$ be the closed geometric point of that factor with the field of $x$, and let $x_{q,i}=(x,a_{q,i})$ be the resulting geometric point of $X_{P_q}=X\times_SP_q$. Use the canonical identification $H_{q,i}\simeq(P_q)_{(a_{q,i})}$ to define
$$c_{q,i}:(P_q)_{(p_i)}\longrightarrow H_{q,i}\simeq(P_q)_{(a_{q,i})}.$$
Thus $c_{q,i}$ is the structural map to $P_q$ factored through the open-and-closed factor $H_{q,i}$. Put $z_{q,i}=(x_{q,i},p_i,c_{q,i})\in V_{f_{P_q}}$ and
$$M_{q,i}:=(X_{P_q})_{(x_{q,i})}\times_{(P_q)_{(a_{q,i})}}(P_q)_{(p_i)}.$$
For $j\in J_q=\pi_0((Q_q)_{b_U})$ define $p^U_j$ as the projection of the unique geometric point of that component with the field of $b_U$. Let $H^U_{q,j}$ be the finite strictly henselian local factor of $Q_q$ containing its image, let $a^U_{q,j}$ be that factor's closed geometric point with the field of $x_U$, and set $x^U_{q,j}=(x_U,a^U_{q,j})\in X_U\times_UQ_q=X_{Q_q}$. Let $c^U_{q,j}:(Q_q)_{(p^U_j)}\to H^U_{q,j}\simeq(Q_q)_{(a^U_{q,j})}$ be the factored structural map. Define $z^U_{q,j}=(x^U_{q,j},p^U_j,c^U_{q,j})\in V_{f_{Q_q}}$ and
$$N_{q,j}:=(X_{Q_q})_{(x^U_{q,j})}\times_{(Q_q)_{(a^U_{q,j})}}(Q_q)_{(p^U_j)}.$$
There are canonical finite disjoint-union identifications
$$M\times_{S_0}P_q=\coprod_{i\in I_q}M_{q,i},\qquad N\times_{U_0}Q_q=\coprod_{j\in J_q}N_{q,j}.$$
The resulting derived section decompositions are finite products. Whenever projection identifies $J_q$ bijectively with $I_q$, the map $A_q\to B_q$ is the product of the stalks of the ordinary comparisons for the Cartesian squares with base map $Q_q\to P_q$, coefficient the pullback of $K$, and the corresponding lifted specializations. These are identifications of the actual restriction maps, compatible with their cofaces; no base-change invertibility or truncated descent is assumed.

source.place: Lemma 2.6 and Lemma 2.6.1, printed pp. 4--5; author PDF read online; archive WANTED. The bounded-complex and map identification are the derived restriction construction, detailed in report.md.

proof.text: The functorial maps $(X_U)_{(x_U)}\to X_{(x)}$, $U_0\to S_0$, and $U_{(b_U)}\to S_{(b)}$ commute with $c_U$ and $c$ because $z_U$ has image $z$. The fibre-product universal property therefore gives $N\to M$. To identify the comparison, use the site triples of the nearby-cycle definition. For a pointed triple $D=(E\to V\leftarrow W)$ at $z$, the inverse image under $\psi_f$ is $E\times_VW$; its pullback triple at $z_U$ has inverse image mapping to $E\times_VW$. On an ordinary sheaf $F$, the transpose of the counit defining $\beta$ sends a section on $E\times_VW$ to its pullback on that inverse image. Indeed evaluation after the counit is restriction to that object, and the adjunction transpose is the unique sheaf map with this evaluation. Composing with the maps from $M$ and $N$ to these objects, the two restrictions agree: both send the section to its pullback by $N\to M\to E\times_VW$, since their two projections agree. Passing over all pointed triples gives the same equality on their filtered stalk colimits. The point-cohomology isomorphism is, by its statement, induced by these restriction maps to the inverse-limit tube, so this proves the equality for its specific normalization, without positing naturality in arbitrary restrictions. The same equality holds termwise on a K-injective representative of $K$; applying the derived comparison to the target complex and then localizing preserves it, by the K-injective definition of $R\Psi$ in the nearby-cycle definition and the construction of $R\Gamma$ in the point-cohomology statement. This identifies $z_U^*\beta_g$ with $R\Gamma(M,K)\to R\Gamma(N,K_U)$.

source.place: Lemma 2.6, first paragraph (pointwise restriction description); the affine-neighbourhood restriction construction and strict-local functoriality are expanded from the cited nodes

proof.text: Identify the base of each tube with a strict localization of $S_0$. Let $b'$ be the closed geometric point of $S_{(b)}$, so the lift of $b$ to $S_0$ is $c\circ b'$. The maps $S_0\to S$ and $S_{(b)}\to S$ are strict-localization structural maps, so the ind-etale strict-local invariance lemma makes the functorial maps $\alpha:(S_0)_{(b)}\to S_{(b)}$ and $j:(S_{(b)})_{(b')}\to S_{(b)}$ isomorphisms, $j$ being the structural map. Let $\gamma:(S_{(b)})_{(b')}\to(S_0)_{(b)}$ be the functorial map of $c$. By the uniqueness clause of the functoriality lemma, $\alpha\circ\gamma$ is the functorial map of the composite $S_{(b)}\to S_0\to S$, which is the structural map of $S_{(b)}$ because $c$ is an $S$-morphism; so $\alpha\circ\gamma=j$ and $\gamma$ is an isomorphism. Moreover $j_{S_0}\circ\gamma=c\circ j$ by that clause. Hence $S_{(b)}$, mapped to $S_0$ by $c$, is $(S_0)_{(b)}$ with its structural map, over $S_0$. At the closed geometric point $a$, the first isomorphism of the strict-base-closed-point-localizations lemma (with $X=S$) gives $(S_0)_{(a)}=S_0$. The same argument, with $(U,U_0,b_U,c_U,a_U)$ in place of $(S,S_0,b,c,a)$, identifies $U_{(b_U)}$ with $(U_0)_{(b_U)}$ over $U_0$ and gives $(U_0)_{(a_U)}=U_0$.

source.place: Lemma 2.6.1, printed p. 5: the tube base S_(b) over S_0 = S_(f(x)); the identification with the strict localization of S_0 is written out here by the maintainer reader from the cited ind-etale invariance and functoriality lemmas

proof.text:
Finite base change and composition make every $P_q\to S_0$ and $Q_q\to U_0$ finite. Using the identification of the preceding step, apply the first clause of the finite-base strict-localization lemma at $b$:
$$S_{(b)}\times_{S_0}P_q\simeq\coprod_{i\in I_q}(P_q)_{(p_i)}.$$
Base change this coproduct by $X_{(x)}\to S_0$ and reassociate the fibre products to obtain
$$M\times_{S_0}P_q\simeq\coprod_i X_{(x)}\times_{S_0}(P_q)_{(p_i)}.$$
For a fixed $i$, apply the same lemma at the closed point $a$ of $S_0$. Since $(S_0)_{(a)}=S_0$ by the preceding step, it gives the open-and-closed strictly local factor $H_{q,i}\simeq(P_q)_{(a_{q,i})}$ containing $p_i$, as used in the statement. Its residue extension over $a$ is finite purely inseparable, so its closed point has a unique lift with the algebraically closed field of $x$: existence follows by taking roots in that field, and uniqueness because a purely inseparable element satisfies a power equation $T^{p^e}-a$ with at most one root; this defines $x_{q,i}=(x,a_{q,i})$. The second clause of the lemma, with finite morphism $P_q\to S_0$ and $Y=X\times_SS_0$, gives
$$(X_{P_q})_{(x_{q,i})}\simeq X_{(x)}\times_{S_0}(P_q)_{(a_{q,i})}.$$
Here strict localization of $X\times_SS_0$ at its closed-fibre lift is $X_{(x)}$ by the strict-base-closed-point-localizations lemma, whose strict-base hypothesis now holds exactly. Pulling this equality back along $c_{q,i}$ cancels the $(P_q)_{(a_{q,i})}$ factor, giving $M_{q,i}\simeq X_{(x)}\times_{S_0}(P_q)_{(p_i)}$. These are the desired factors. Replacing $(S_0,X_{(x)},P_q,b)$ by $(U_0,(X_U)_{(x_U)},Q_q,b_U)$ repeats each of the displayed equalities and gives the asserted decomposition for $N$.

source.place: Lemma 2.6.1, printed p. 5: finite-cover fibre components and Milnor-tube decomposition, with the finite-local-factor calculation supplied by Tags 04GH and 0GIP

proof.text: Sections of a sheaf complex over a finite disjoint union are the finite product of the sections over its components; the same holds after taking derived sections because finite products of module complexes are finite direct sums and are exact. Thus the preceding decompositions give the stated finite-product descriptions of $(A_q)$ and $(B_q)$, and restriction maps in the augmented Cech diagrams are componentwise restrictions.

source.place: Lemma 2.6 and Lemma 2.6.1, pp. 4--5 (sections over the finite component decomposition)

proof.text:
Projection gives $J_q\simeq I_q$ by the component lemma. Choose the geometric points compatibly with projection, which is possible by taking their fields to be those of $b_U$ and $b$. For $j\mapsto i$, the structural map $Q_q\to P_q$ sends the factor $H^U_{q,j}$ into $H_{q,i}$: the inverse image of an open-and-closed factor is open and closed, and the connected scheme $H^U_{q,j}$ meets that inverse image at $p^U_j$. It sends its closed point to the closed point of $H_{q,i}$, since $U_0\to S_0$ is local and the closed fibre of each finite strictly local factor is a singleton. Consequently $x^U_{q,j}$ maps to $x_{q,i}$, and the square of the factored structural maps $c^U_{q,j},c_{q,i}$ commutes. Under the projection-preserving identifications in Step 3, the component tube map is
$$(X_U)_{(x_U)}\times_{U_0}(Q_q)_{(p^U_j)}\longrightarrow X_{(x)}\times_{S_0}(P_q)_{(p_i)},$$
with projections the canonical strict-local maps. These are also the projections of the tube map for the cartesian square with base $Q_q\to P_q$, by functoriality of strict localizations; fibre-product uniqueness makes the two maps equal. Step 1 applied to this square therefore identifies each component restriction with its ordinary comparison stalk. For a Cech face or degeneracy, the two candidate composites have the same projections to the strict-local $X$-factor and to the finite-cover factor: these are precisely the identities between projections and repeated coordinates defining the Cech nerve. Fibre-product uniqueness again makes them equal. Applying derived sections gives compatibility of the finite-product maps with cofaces and degeneracies, as claimed.
